answerBody:
Congress should enact the 20-megawatt incremental-cost floor, not the size-neutral rewrite of FERC's 1994 transmission pricing policy, as the governing rule for data-center grid charges before the new Congress convenes.

The two rules inside Section 2107 of S. 5653 are not interchangeable versions of cost causation. Foley Hoag's analysis of the September 30 introduced text separates them. Subsection (a) would force FERC, within 270 days, to revise the October 26, 1994 Transmission Pricing Policy Statement so computational loads pay both embedded transmission costs and incremental expansion costs, with no megawatt cutoff. Subsection (b) would add Federal Power Act section 228. For covered computing loads of 20 megawatts or more, including phased and commonly controlled multi-site loads, it would bar shifting incremental generation, storage, transmission, and distribution costs onto other customers, require financial assurances before upgrades, and continue recovery if the load leaves.

The floor matches the harm households face. A data center's distinctive cost is the plant and wires that would not exist but for that load. The floor assigns that avoidable cost across the supply chain, and it is a minimum: FERC or a state may charge more and credit the surplus. It also preserves state tools, including open seasons and bring-your-own generation, without rewriting wholesale transmission doctrine.

The size-neutral rewrite fails that test. FERC's 1994 policy rejected "and" pricing because embedded and incremental charges were alternative measures of the same transmission capacity. Findings that any lower charge is not just and reasonable would lock the opposite theory into the rate standard for every computational site, including loads too small for a special class. The revenue-requirement credit is only a partial answer, because rolled-in embedded rates already contain prior expansions. FERC would still untangle that overlap in a rule that could take about two and a half years. If charges are high enough, loads can self-supply, and a late mandate does not protect the customers who remain.

The strongest counterargument is Ari Peskoe's, set out in Utility Dive in April 2026 and quantified by Grid Strategies in November. The 1994 ban was written to stop utilities from overcharging competing generators, not to subsidize new consumers. Under a narrow "higher of" reading, a load that triggers an expensive upgrade pays only the larger number and can leave either its network share or its upgrade cost on everyone else. Grid Strategies estimates the rewrite would collect about $55 billion over ten years, roughly $35 billion more than current policy, on 40.3 gigawatts outside ERCOT assuming firm service. That gap is real, but transmission-only. The same paper treats the floor's broader costs as a much larger pool, an upper bound near $136 billion if states use it. Choosing the floor does not forfeit embedded-cost charges. It refuses to make stacked transmission pricing the national rule while generation and distribution remain assignable.

Congress should enact the 20-megawatt floor, with assurances and continued recovery, as the governing cost rule now, and leave the 1994 policy intact.
rationale: The follow-on question forces a choice between two cost rules inside S. 5653 Section 2107, not a repeat of the prior hold-or-pass debate. Foley Hoag's reading of the September 30 introduced text, Grid Strategies' November white paper as reported by Daily Energy Insider, and FERC's 1994 rejection of and-pricing support choosing the 20-megawatt floor: it covers generation, storage, transmission, and distribution, includes assurances, and avoids locking stacked transmission charges into the just-and-reasonable standard for every computational load. Peskoe's higher-of critique and the $55 billion estimate are treated as the strongest counterargument and judged transmission-only. The word-counting capability confirmed answerBody is within range.
